metrics.claim_path: no-llm/no-network (structural; the fast claim check is a local HMAC verify)

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).
findings.suggested_fix: Split compound criteria, replace subjective terms with observable outcomes, and state how each is verified.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Capture the one-gate resolution rule and the rejected `--gate` flag alternative in an ADR, AGENTS.md section, or inline design comment durable enough for future gate authors to discover.
evidence: Plan introduces the 'active in exactly one gate ⇒ resolve there' rule as a new architectural policy for CLI preflight dispatch
No mention of ADR, AGENTS.md, or design doc update in Scope or anywhere in the plan
Rejected alternative section exists but is prose-only, not captured in a durable artifact
findings.finding: The plan introduces a new cross-component architectural decision — dual-registry admission with one-gate resolution as the CLI dispatch rule — but specifies no update to an ADR, AGENTS.md, or design doc to capture this pattern. Future authors adding a third gate will have no documented rationale for why the one-gate rule exists or how to extend it.
scenarios: A third gate is added to the system; a future author extends the preflight without understanding the one-gate rule's rationale, introducing inconsistent behavior
A reviewer questions why ambiguity is rejected rather than prompted, finds no durable record of the decision
findings.suggested_fix: Add a brief ADR entry (or a AGENTS.md paragraph under the `criteria eval` section) stating: 'The CLI preflight resolves criterion IDs by looking up both plan-review and code-review registries; an ID present in exactly one gate is dispatched there; presence in both is rejected as ambiguous. A `--gate` flag was rejected as heavier UX for a rare case.' This anchors the invariant for future gate authors.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify (and test) error handling for `code_review.registry.effective_criteria(repo_root)` failures — at minimum, catch registry-read exceptions and emit a clear CLI error message (exit 1) consistent with the existing error-handling style in `_llm_eval_commands.py`.
evidence: 'Look the id up in BOTH the plan-review effective registry and the code-review effective registry (`code_review.registry.effective_criteria(repo_root)`)' — no error handling mentioned
Testing section covers only happy-path, unknown, and ambiguous outcomes; no test for registry-read failure
Existing plan-review path's error handling behavior is not extended to the new code-review lookup in the plan text
findings.finding: The plan adds a call to `code_review.registry.effective_criteria(repo_root)` — a file-I/O operation reading config from disk — but specifies no error handling for the case where that call raises (e.g., malformed config, missing activation file, permission error). An unhandled exception here would surface as a raw traceback instead of a clean CLI error message.
scenarios: The repo's code-review activation config is malformed; the CLI crashes with a traceback instead of a helpful message
The repo_root path lacks read permissions; the user sees an unhandled OSError rather than a clear diagnostic
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the `effective_criteria` call in a try/except that catches registry-read errors (e.g., `RegistryLoadError` or `OSError`) and emits a message like `'error: could not load code-review registry: {e}'` before exiting 1, mirroring however the plan-review registry lookup is already guarded.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a positive rationale sentence to the Approach section explaining WHY dual-registry admission at the CLI preflight boundary is the right fit (e.g., it reuses the already-landed effective_criteria and calibrate_criterion seams from child 4 without altering their interfaces, and keeps gate-resolution logic at the caller boundary layer).
evidence: The Approach section's only rationale statement is: 'Adding a criteria eval --gate flag — heavier UX for a rare case; the "active in exactly one gate ⇒ resolve there" rule covers the common path and only genuine cross-gate ambiguity needs operator input.' This explains why NOT to do the alternative, not why TO do the chosen approach.
No sentence in the plan affirmatively states why dual-registry admission at the CLI boundary is the right architectural fit for this codebase.
findings.finding: The plan provides only a negative rationale for the chosen approach (the rejected '--gate flag' alternative is called 'heavier UX for a rare case') but never states a positive rationale for why dual-registry admission at the CLI preflight boundary is the right fit — e.g., that it reuses the already-landed registry seams (child 4's effective_criteria + calibrate_criterion gate-aware arm), keeps gate logic at the caller/boundary layer, and requires no change to the calibrate_criterion interface or its callers. The rubric (G6 criterion 4) requires the plan to assert a positive rationale for the chosen approach; its absence is a finding.
scenarios: An implementer reading only the plan cannot understand what design principle they should preserve when making tradeoffs — they have justification for rejecting one alternative but no anchor for the chosen approach.
findings.suggested_fix: Append to the Approach section: 'This boundary-layer approach reuses the gate-aware seams already landed by child 4 (effective_criteria and calibrate_criterion) without altering their interfaces or adding new library-level coupling — the CLI preflight is the correct authority for id disambiguation because it owns the user-facing error surface and has access to both registry namespaces through the same repo_root context it already resolves.'
